report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Conventionality and transparency in human language

author.affiliation:
Center for Brain and Cognition

text.text: The most distinctive feature of language is perhaps the ability to produce and comprehend utterances that have never been said before.
This requires language to be transparent: comprehenders can infer the meaning of an utterance based on its components and the rules used to combine them.
However, arbitrary associations between form and meaning (conventionality) are ubiquitous in language, despite them being difficult to learn.
This is true for words, but also for many utterances.
Why is this the case?
In this paper, we propose languages balance conventionality and transparency by minimizing the communication and learning cost.
While transparency facilitates learnability and comprehensibility, encoding every meaning transparently inevitably results in longer words, which raises the communication cost.

On the other hand, conventionality enables meanings to be encoded arbitrarily, allowing more frequent meanings to have shorter words, which minimizes the communication cost, but it also makes words and utterances more opaque, thus increasing understanding and learning cost.
We hypothesized that more frequent words are more likely to be conventionalized.
We also hypothesized communities with a higher degree of shared exposure to the common ground tend to have a higher proportion of conventionalized words.
First, we conducted a cost-minimizing simulation, and the results supported both hypotheses.

Then, we empirically tested the first hypothesis, using a novel metric on semantic transparency, and we found support to it, since more frequent words in English are indeed less semantically transparent.
Overall, our findings support a trade-off between conventionality and transparency in human languages.
Is "moonshine" the light from the moon?

An English speaker who has never drunk alcohol may say yes, because by following the meaning of its parts and rules of forming compound nouns in English, the resultant interpretation will indeed be "the light of the moon".
However, the main meaning of moonshine is not transparent, as it cannot be deduced by combining individual morphemes in the word.
Instead, the meaning is conventionalized, as language users mutually agree that "moonshine" refers to a type of liquor, not the light from the moon.

Conventionalization occurs in other levels of grammar, too: the phrase "long island iced tea" is a cocktail instead of a kind of iced tea, and the idiom "the ball is in your court" doesn't mean there is a physical ball in your court, but it means it is your turn to take actions.
Why do languages have conventionalized expressions?

Conventionalization seems to interfere with perhaps the central design feature of language: the ability to generate and interpret new utterances that have never been said before (Chomsky, 1957; Hockett, 1960).
text.formatted: Conventionalization seems to interfere with perhaps the central design feature of language: the ability to generate and interpret new utterances that have never been said before <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chomsky, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hockett, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: This is only possible if languages are transparent, so that the meaning of an unfamiliar word or utterance can be inferred from its form, specifically from the meaning of its parts and the rules used for combining them.
Conventionalization, however, typically makes inferring meaning of unseen sentences difficult or impossible.
In addition, conventionalization also seems to make languages more difficult to learn, since the form-meaning pairing needs to be learned one by one.

Studies with artificial languages whose meanings are more inferrable from forms suggest that they are indeed easier to learn for adults (Raviv et al., 2021) and for deep neural networks (Galke et al., 2024).

text.text: This also explains why learners usually regularize an artificial language over the course of an experiment (Smith et al., 2023), and why compositional structure appears in them as an emergent property as they are transmitted (Kirby et al., 2015; Saldana et al., 2019; Kirby and Tamariz, 2022).
text.formatted: This also explains why learners usually regularize an artificial language over the course of an experiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Smith et al., 2023)</ref>, and why compositional structure appears in them as an emergent property as they are transmitted <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kirby et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Saldana et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kirby and Tamariz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Regular forms are more transparent, whereas irregular forms are more conventionalized.
Accordingly, if transparency facilitates productivity, comprehensibility, and learnability, why do languages contain so many conventionalized forms that are opaque to diverse degrees?
A possible answer is that conventionalization has also some advantages.
In particular, it enables languages to pair forms and meanings in more efficient ways from a communicative perspective.
This typically happens when meanings are packaged in shorter forms, which are easier to utter.

For example, college students often shorten the transparent phrase "organic chemistry" to simply "orgo", so that the whole phrase is reduced to the first two syllables of the first word, even though "orgo" is opaque.
Many studies show that languages are indeed shaped by this pressure towards communicative efficiency (See Gibson et al., 2019, for a review).
text.formatted: Many studies show that languages are indeed shaped by this pressure towards communicative efficiency (See <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gibson et al., 2019</ref>, for a review).

text.text: Ample evidence suggests, specifically, that more frequent words tend to be shorter in length, like "orgo" for students of organic chemistry (e.g. Estoup, 1912; Zipf, 1936; Piantadosi et al., 2011; Levshina, 2022).
text.formatted: Ample evidence suggests, specifically, that more frequent words tend to be shorter in length, like "orgo" for students of organic chemistry (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Estoup, 1912;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Zipf, 1936;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Piantadosi et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Levshina, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In this way, the expected number of sounds speakers need to Draft utter can be reduced.
However, shorter lengths also limit the number of meaningful units a word can carry to be interpretable, which puts an upper bound on a word's transparency.

This is possibly why cross-linguistically, strongly synthetic languages tend to be agglutinative instead of fusional, since in the latter type one single morpheme typically conveys several grammatical information (Greenberg, 1960).
text.formatted: This is possibly why cross-linguistically, strongly synthetic languages tend to be agglutinative instead of fusional, since in the latter type one single morpheme typically conveys several grammatical information <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Greenberg, 1960)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, we argue that languages balance two costs: a production/communication cost (how long utterances take to be generated) and an understanding/learning cost (how hard form-meaning pairings are to be understood/acquired).
Conventionalization lowers production/communication cost by allowing short, arbitrary forms, whereas transparency lowers understanding/learning cost by making meaning inferable from form.
How do languages balance conventionality and transparency?

Conventionalization depends on repeated exposure (since conventionalized forms are more difficult to understand and learn because of their opacity) and shared exposure (since a convention cannot be one if it is not shared among many people).

In addition, words within a language do not distribute uniformly in frequency: a small number of words appear very frequently, whereas a large number of words are relatively scarce (Estoup, 1912; Zipf, 1936).
text.formatted: In addition, words within a language do not distribute uniformly in frequency: a small number of words appear very frequently, whereas a large number of words are relatively scarce <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Estoup, 1912;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Zipf, 1936)</ref>.

text.text: A way for languages to balance between conventionalization and transparency is to make higher frequency words conventional and lower frequency words transparent.
In this way, higher frequency words can be be shorter, and the average message length becomes reduced.

But because higher frequency words tend to appear frequently (by definition), they also tend to be more widely known among speakers (Brysbaert et al., 2019), are evoked more easily in the mind (Polich and Donchin, 1988), and are acquired earlier, particularly by children (Ambridge et al., 2015; Wray, 2002).

text.text: The ultimate reason is the repeated exposure to them.
Conversely, making lower frequency words transparent enables meanings to be easier inferrable from forms, in spite of the limited exposure to them.
At the same time, as they are relatively infrequent, the overall length of the utterance does not increase excessively.
Past studies support this trade-off between high-and low-frequency items in some specific aspects of grammar.

For example, high frequency verbs in English tend to have more irregular (i.e. more opaque and shorter) past tenses (e.g. "run" -"ran"), whereas low frequency ones tend to have regular (i.e. more transparent and longer) past tenses (e.g. "devour" -"devoured", Marcus et al., 1992; Haspelmath and Sims, 2002; Cuskley et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019).

text.text: However, it is still unclear whether such a finding generalizes to all words.
This gives rise to our first hypothesis: less frequent words tend to be more semantically transparent, across the whole lexicon.
Besides frequency, a second property that could impact the conventionalization of utterances in a language is, as noted, the amount of shared exposure in its speakers.
As characterized in Thurston (1989); Wray and Grace (2007), communications in a community can be either towards esotericity (i.e. inwardorienting) or towards exotericity (i.e. outward-orienting).

text.text: Members of an esoteric community tend to communicate only with other members within the same community, who accordingly share the same culture and environment.
On the other hand, members of an exoteric community tend to communicate more with outsiders, who tend to live in a different physical and/or cultural environment.

Therefore, the amount of common knowledge (i.e. shared exposure) in these two types of community differs: members of an esoteric community tend to have a higher degree of shared exposure, and those of an exoteric community tend to have a lower degree of shared exposure. Wray and Grace (2007) hypothesizes that languages spoken by esoteric communities tend to be more conventionalized, whereas those spoken by exoteric communities tend to be more transparent.

text.text: For instance, the languages spoken by exoteric communities tend to encode case or tense transparently as separate words instead of inflectional (and frequently opaque) affixes, which are more common in the languages spoken by esoteric communities.
This differential language transparency depending on sociopolitical features could ultimately result from minimizing their total communication and learning cost.

An exoteric community with a low degree of shared exposure means that it is unlikely for a random listener to know an opaque form-meaning pairing except for the most frequent words, so conventionalizing further into lower frequency meanings incurs a high learning and repair cost.

On the other hand, a random listener in an esoteric community is likely to know the opaque form-meaning pairing even for low frequency words, and therefore, the language can prioritize conventionality to minimize the expected message length.

Taken together, our second hypothesis is that the more esoteric the society, the higher proportion of conventionalized words, and the more exoteric the society, the higher proportion of semantically transparent words.
This paper provides support for both hypotheses.

text.text: In the second analysis, which is a corpus analysis, we investigated the degree of conventionalization of words in natural languages (English and Greek) as a function of their frequency.
We operationalized conventionality as to what extent a word's meaning can be inferred from its spelling alone.
We found that higher frequency English and Greek words tend to be more conventionalized than lower frequency English and Greek words.

In this analysis, we simulate the combination of conventionality and transparency that minimizes the communication and learning cost of a language, given a degree of shared exposure within a community.
In the simulation, there are a total of 1000 unique meanings to be expressed in words within a community.
We assume everyone in the community is an adult and is familiar with the morphemes of the language.
These meanings are distributed in a Zipfian manner: a meaning's occurrence frequency is inversely proportional to its rank.
A meaning can be encoded in the lexicon in two ways: a transparent encoding and a conventional encoding, and each encoding is associated with a communication cost and a learning cost.

A key assumption in our analysis is that the transparent encoding has a higher communication cost than the conventional encoding, as transparent word usually include more than one morpheme and are hence usually longer (e.g. "automobile" vs. "car").
Another key assumption is that the communication cost is incurred every time the word is uttered, but the learning cost is only incurred one time.
Despite the high communication cost, in the transparent encoding, someone that has not been exposed to the word can understand it, so it has a learning cost of 0.
On the other hand, the conventionalized encoding has a lower communication cost, but a person who has not been exposed to the lexicon will not be able to understand it.
To be learned, the word has to be listened several times, and/or the meaning has to be said again in a transparent way, which add to the communication cost.
Then a learning cost is incurred when the person learns the word.

text.text: The all-transparent encoding has a flat cost, regardless of degrees of exposure.

The all-conventional encoding has a high cost for communities with low shared exposure, since in these communities, people are unlikely to know the meaning of conventionalized words, and hence they have to repeat them and/or rephrase them with the transparent form.
Then, as the degree of shared exposure increases, the cost for all-conventional encoding drops, since repeats and repairs occur less frequently.
Interestingly, for highly esoteric communities with a high degree of shared exposure, the cost all-conventional encoding increases again.
This is because people in these communities must learn the form-meaning pairing of words which are rarely used, making it not worth the effort to learn.

Results from the simulation are so far consistent with our hypotheses: first, among all communities, lower frequency words are more semantically transparent; and second, more exoteric communities tend to have a higher proportion of transparent words.
Now the question is whether the same results hold for real data.
In the next part of the paper, we test the first prediction on English words, using a novel formulation of semantic transparency.
In this analysis, we measure the semantic transparency of a list of written English words, as a function of their frequency.
Here we defined semantic transparency as the extent to which a model can infer a word's meaning based on its orthography, compared to an orthography-blind baseline.
To ensure the model is not inferring a word's meaning simply by memorizing its spelling, we divided the word list into five folds.

For a word w, the remaining four folds were the training set T , and w's fold was the held-out set E. All the quantities below, such as the meaning vector of the word m w and the feature vector of the word v w , were estimated based on the training set T and then applied to the held-out set E.
We represented a word's meaning m w using GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), a model pretrained on Wikipedia and Gigaword, where a word is represented by a 50-dimensional vector.
text.formatted: We represented a word's meaning m w using GloVe <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Pennington et al., 2014)</ref>, a model pretrained on Wikipedia and Gigaword, where a word is represented by a 50-dimensional vector.

text.text: Importantly, words that are closer together in the vector space have similar meanings.
Following Mu et al. (2017), in order to eliminate information irrelevant to word semantics, such as word frequency, we centered the raw GloVe vectors and removed the top-2 principal components.

text.text: The mean and the principal components were estimated from the training set T .
The vectors were L2-normalized afterwards.
We represented a word's orthography by a feature vector.
Each dimension of the feature vector is an n-gram that occurred in the training set T , where n ∈ [2, 5].

The value of each dimension is the L2-normalized term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf) weight of the correspond-Draft ing n-gram (Spärck Jones, 1972), computed among words in the training set.

The inferred meaning of word w in the held-out set, mT (w), is computed by a Ridge regression (α = 8) trained on words in the training set T .
The similarity between the inferred meaning and the actual meaning is given by the cosine distance between mT (w) and m w .
As an orthography-blind baseline, we also computed the similarity as the cosine distance between the mean of the training set µ T and m w.

A higher δ(w) indicates a higher transparency, as the model that has never seen the word w can infer its meaning strictly from its orthography.

Meanwhile, a lower δ(w) suggests a lower transparency, as the model is not good at inferring the meaning of the word w based on its orthography, especially when δ(w) < 0, which means that the model is worse than the orthography-blind baseline.

text.text: We selected three databases of English words.
LADEC (Gagné et al., 2019) is a database of 8376 English compound words.

text.text: All the words in the database can be segmented into two constituents that are themselves free words (in turn, such words can contain one or more morphemes; e.g. playwrights → play + wrights; wrights → wright + s).
We removed all the incorrect segmentations, words that are not in our GloVe word list, and words without a frequency entry, which left us with 4372 words in this database.
The second database we included was MorphoLex (Sánchez-Gutiérrez et al., 2018), a database of 68000 English words.

The third database in our analysis was SUBTLEX-US (Brysbaert and New, 2009), a database of 60000 English words.

text.text: The regression above did not account for one confound: hubness (Radovanovic et al., 2010; Ethayarajh, 2019), which refers to the phenomenon that some words have more close neighbors than others.
text.formatted: The regression above did not account for one confound: hubness <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Radovanovic et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Ethayarajh, 2019)</ref>, which refers to the phenomenon that some words have more close neighbors than others.

text.text: The transparency score of a word with many close neighbors (a "hub") can be inflated, because a hub tends to be located at the center of a cluster, which is also what our model tends to predict when it does not have enough clues.
This means that a hub can have a high transparency score by coincidence, rather than by actually being semantically transparent.
To account for this, we also operationalized hubness as the average cosine distance between a word and its five closest neighbors in the meaning space.

After adding hubness as a predictor in our linear regression model, we found a negative effect of frequency on transparency score in all three datasets (β = -0.023, p < 0.001 for LADEC; β=-0.060, p <0.001 for MorphoLex; and β = -0.060, p <0.001 for SUBTLEX-US).

text.text: Languages seek to strike a balance between two objectives.
On one hand, they need to be communicatively efficient (Gibson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: On one hand, they need to be communicatively efficient <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gibson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: One way to achieve this is by making more frequently used words shorter (Zipf, 1936; Estoup, 1912; Piantadosi et al., 2011).
text.formatted: One way to achieve this is by making more frequently used words shorter <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Zipf, 1936;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Estoup, 1912;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Piantadosi et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, they need to be easy to understand and learn.
One way to achieve this is by making word forms reflective of the word's meaning (Raviv et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2023; Galke et al., 2024).
text.formatted: One way to achieve this is by making word forms reflective of the word's meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Raviv et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Smith et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Galke et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, such two objectives cannot be achieved at the same time: encoding the most frequent meaning with the shortest symbol does not ensure transparency, because transparency requires a word's meaning to be built from meaningful parts, which requires length, but it is difficult for short words to have room for such structure.
Conversely, making words more transparent usually results in longer words that are more costly to utter.
How do languages balance these two goals?
We hypothesize that languages make more frequent words conventional and less frequent words transparent, and in this way, languages can minimize the communication and learning cost.

We also hypothesize that different types of communities have different splits of conventionalization and transparency: more esoteric communities, characterized by a high degree of shared exposure, have more conventionalized words than more exoteric communities, which are characterized by a low degree of shared exposure.
We conducted two analyses.

First, we performed a simulation in order to find the combination of conventionality and transparency that minimizes the communication and learning cost of a community, given a degree of common exposure.
The results are consistent with both of our hypothe- ses.

Second, we tested our first hypothesis on three datasets in English, and one dataset in Greek, using a novel metric of semantic transparency, and the results are also as predicted: more frequent words in both languages tend to be less semantically transparent.
In our opinion, our study has some merits (not without some limitations).
First, we introduced a novel metric for semantic transparency, formulated as the extent to which a word's meaning can be inferred solely from its orthography.
Accordingly, our metric computes a transparency score directly from a word's spelling, which is particularly useful for corpus analyses.
Furthermore, it does not involve human rating (e.g.
LADEC, Gagné et al., 2019), which may be noisy.
text.formatted: LADEC, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gagné et al., 2019)</ref>, which may be noisy.

text.text: It does not involve morpheme segmentation (e.g.
CELEX, Baayen et al., 1996) either, as it bypasses the morpheme level entirely.
text.formatted: CELEX, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baayen et al., 1996)</ref> either, as it bypasses the morpheme level entirely.

text.text: Finally, our metric is able to capture regularities that exist below the morpheme level, such as phonesthemes (Firth and Strevens, 1968) or morphemes borrowed from other languages.
text.formatted: Finally, our metric is able to capture regularities that exist below the morpheme level, such as phonesthemes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Firth and Strevens, 1968</ref>) or morphemes borrowed from other languages.

text.text: With our novel metric, our study is also the first to directly test the degree of word transparency as a function of word frequency at a lexical level.
Previous studies (e.g. Cuskley et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019) were mainly focused on the morphological level, since they tested the regularity of word inflection as a function of frequency.
text.formatted: Previous studies (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cuskley et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Wu et al., 2019)</ref> were mainly focused on the morphological level, since they tested the regularity of word inflection as a function of frequency.

text.text: Here we extended the notion of inflectional regularity to semantic transparency more generally, and asked to what extent a word's meaning, besides merely the inflected form, can be inferred from a word's orthography.

We thus speculate that opacity, or irregularity in this case, allows a shorter or a more distinctive form, thus minimizing the average signal length or reducing the chance of miscommunication, both of which are beneficial to communicative efficiency.
This is clearly observed in irregular verbs: irregular forms are shorter (e.g. "sang" instead of "*singed") and more distinctive (e.g. "went" instead of "*goed").
This approach can be potentially extended beyond the word to opaque word chunks, like idioms.
Additionally, our study also sheds lights on how words are organized to facilitate usage.

Many past studies have shown that there exists a trade-off between accuracy and simplicity in the mapping between form and meaning (e.g. Zaslavsky et al., 2018): achieving a higher accuracy requires a higher level of complexity, or putting this differently, more distinct labels are required in order to talk about things more accurately.
text.formatted: Many past studies have shown that there exists a trade-off between accuracy and simplicity in the mapping between form and meaning (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Zaslavsky et al., 2018)</ref>: achieving a higher accuracy requires a higher level of complexity, or putting this differently, more distinct labels are required in order to talk about things more accurately.

text.text: Transparency is a way to provide labels to meanings that are easier to learn and use.

However, some meanings are talked about more than others, so the more frequent a meaning, the more important to keep its label relatively short, since keeping labels short reduces the average message length.

Lastly, our study echoes with the hypothesis put forward in Wray and Grace (2007) that languages spoken by esoteric communities tend to exhibit more conventionality, such as more suppletion, semantically opaque idioms, and irregular morphology, by simulating how languages in different types of communities should balance conventionality and transparency to minimize communication and learning cost among members of a community.
text.formatted: Lastly, our study echoes with the hypothesis put forward in <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wray and Grace (2007)</ref> that languages spoken by esoteric communities tend to exhibit more conventionality, such as more suppletion, semantically opaque idioms, and irregular morphology, by simulating how languages in different types of communities should balance conventionality and transparency to minimize communication and learning cost among members of a community.

text.text: We drew insights from Wray and Grace (2007) that members of an esoteric community share more of a culture and environment, whereas those of an exoteric one tends to share less.
text.formatted: We drew insights from <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wray and Grace (2007)</ref> that members of an esoteric community share more of a culture and environment, whereas those of an exoteric one tends to share less.

text.text: Interestingly, our simulation revealed an additional insight: even within a highly esoteric community, there will still be some degree of semantic transparency left, due to the skewed distribution of word frequency, as some words are too infrequent to be worth the learning cost if encoded conventionally.
This is a testable prediction that can be addressed in future studies.
We have not done this in our study, mostly because our metric is not without limitations.
In particular, it is corpus dependent: a word may have a different transparency score under a different training score.
Given this, our transparency score so far cannot be compared across corpora, or across languages.

Accordingly, to test, specifically, our second hypothesis, future work should operationalize the meaning of a word m(w) using a multilingual language Draft model, instead of GloVe in one language, in order to directly compare the degree of transparency across different languages spoken by exoteric and esoteric communities.
Finally, our study mainly focused on conventionalization enabling more frequent meanings to be encoded with shorter words, but conventionalization also has other sociolinguistic effects.
For example, it has been suggested that idioms can signal affiliation of a certain ethnic group (Pitzl, 2022; Ayed, 2008).
text.formatted: For example, it has been suggested that idioms can signal affiliation of a certain ethnic group <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pitzl, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Ayed, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Our approach indeed supports this view: a critical step towards affiliation of a certain ethnic group is the degree of common knowledge resulting from shared exposure with that ethnic group, with idioms being one strong indicator of such shared exposure.

Other studies also suggested that certain creative, non-transparent words (e.g. "spitfire" meaning a person that is easy to provoke) make their creators clever and wittier, potentially making them as more attractive sexual partners (Progovac, 2026).

text.text: Future studies can use our formulation of semantic transparency to evaluate why some non-transparent words are judged as witty but not others.
